source.version: Undated manuscript on file; the PDF does not print a version number, publication date, or journal imprint (p. 1). Retrieval metadata identifies an arXiv source, but a specific arXiv version is not confirmed by the document.
source.title_on_document: Voice-based debate with an AI adversary is associated with increased divergent ideation

supplement.where: Supporting Information, pp. 10-16 of this PDF, referred to as the SI Appendix in the main text (pp. 3, 4 and 6).
supplement.holds: Sample preprocessing and participant exclusions; conversation and voice-gender counts; pooled descriptive statistics and modality-switching checks (p. 10); text preprocessing and measure construction (pp. 11-12); a lexical-diversity word-count-control coefficient absent from Table 1 (p. 11); statistical-analysis details and two illustrative full transcripts (pp. 12-16). Main modality coefficients and clustered SEs are already in Table 1 (p. 9). Neither the main table nor this appendix provides outcome-specific statistics for the randomized voice-gender comparison.

paper_design_summary: MBA and EMBA students debated business strategy cases with the CAiSEY AI adversary, choosing voice or text for each interaction; the main analysis compares 957 conversations from 203 analyzed students using user and case fixed effects (pp. 2-3, Approach; p. 10, Supporting Information). Computed scores on user-only text measure originality relative to the case reading, verbosity, repetition, and semantic breadth within each conversation (pp. 9, 11-12). AI voice gender was randomly assigned within spoken interactions, but its outcome results are reported only as a general statement of no effects (pp. 3, 5 and 10).

studies.label: CAiSEY business-case debates: self-selected communication modality with a nested randomized voice-gender comparison

assignment.what_was_assigned: For the principal voice-versus-text contrast, students opted into CAiSEY and chose their communication modality separately for each case; neither AI availability nor modality/order was randomly assigned (pp. 2-3; p. 10, Modality Switching). A distinct nested manipulation randomly assigned perceived male versus female AI voice when the voice option was chosen (pp. 3 and 10). The no value describes the principal modality contrast, not the nested voice-gender manipulation. The exact unit and repeated-user allocation procedure for the latter are not stated.
assignment.quote: Because users self-selected their communication modality rather than being experimentally assigned, we cannot make strict causal claims regarding the effect of interface choice on discourse structure.
assignment.locator: p. 3, Approach; p. 10, Modality Switching Across Successive CAiSEY Sessions. Mixed structure reflects 186 of 203 users using both modalities, with other users contributing only one modality (p. 3).

arms.name: Voice-based CAiSEY (Walk-and-Talk; both voice genders)
arms.description: Students chose spoken debate with CAiSEY. There are 458 analyzed conversations, not 458 people; exact distinct people in this modality are not reported (p. 10, Descriptive Statistics). This parent condition includes both nested voice-gender conditions.

arms.name: Text-based CAiSEY
arms.description: Students chose typed debate with the same AI adversary, case readings, prompts, and opposition strategy (p. 3). There are 499 analyzed conversations, not 499 people; exact distinct people in this modality are not reported (p. 10).

arms.name: Voice-based CAiSEY: female voice (nested condition)
arms.description: Randomly assigned perceived female AI voice within the spoken condition; 240 conversations, not a reported count of distinct people. Nested within the voice parent condition and not an additional independent arm/sample (pp. 3 and 10).

arms.name: Voice-based CAiSEY: male voice (nested condition)
arms.description: Randomly assigned perceived male AI voice within the spoken condition; 218 conversations, not a reported count of distinct people. Nested within the voice parent condition and not an additional independent arm/sample (pp. 3 and 10).

participants.exclusions: The initial dataset included 224 students; 17 were excluded because they did not use either required CAiSEY modality, and another 4 lacked sufficient data for the word-count-adjusted lexical and semantic diversity measures, yielding 203 analyzed students (p. 10, Sample Preprocessing). The initial count is not a randomized count. Unique people analyzed within each modality or randomized voice-gender contrast are not reported.
participants.who: MBA and EMBA students in an elective Technology Strategy course at a U.S. business school (p. 2, Approach); acknowledgments identify the participating students as Columbia Business School students (p. 6).
participants.quote: The analytic sample consists of 957 independent CAiSEY conversations generated by 203 MBA and EMBA students across 16 case-based assignments.
participants.locator: p. 10, Sample Preprocessing and Descriptive Statistics; p. 2, Approach, for U.S. course setting; p. 6, Acknowledgments. The paper calls conversations independent in this quote, but its regression SEs are clustered by user and case (pp. 9 and 12).

ai_tool.name_model: CAiSEY (Classroom Artificial Intelligence Studio for Engaging You); underlying generative model/version not stated (pp. 2-3, Approach).
ai_tool.how_used: In-house AI debate opponent. A student selected a position and gave an opening argument; CAiSEY automatically argued the opposite position and responded to the student in an extended exchange, through voice or text. It supplied counterarguments/content, so it is not coded as a content-free coach. It remained available while all scored user messages were produced (p. 3, Approach; pp. 12-16, example transcripts).

task.description: Generate and develop arguments and strategic proposals in open-ended debate about assigned business cases. Students read case background, chose a stance, and defended it against the AI interlocutor; for example, which content strategy Netflix should prioritize. The course offered 16 case readings, and AI use for each was optional (pp. 2-3, Approach). The paper explicitly describes debate as having no right answer and benefiting from different arguments (p. 2).
task.duration: Interaction time limit and session duration not stated. Repeated optional interactions occurred over the course term (p. 2, Approach).

outcomes.name: Divergent ideation: within-conversation semantic diversity (word-count adjusted; raw variant retained)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: All text measures use concatenated user messages only, excluding AI messages (p. 11, Text Extraction). One analysis observation is one conversation, with repeated conversations per student; the analytic sample contains 957 conversations from 203 students (p. 10, Descriptive Statistics). Table 1 uses OLS with user and case fixed effects and standard errors clustered by user and case (pp. 9 and 12, Statistical Analyses). The paper operationalizes breadth of a single user's ideas, not diversity across different people. Cleaned user text is split into overlapping 50-word chunks with a 25-word step (50% overlap); all-MiniLM-L6-v2 encodes each chunk into 384 dimensions. Pairwise chunk cosine similarities, excluding the diagonal, are clipped to [0, 1], normalized to probabilities, and summarized using Shannon entropy. This compares chunks within one conversation. The primary score residualizes semantic diversity with respect to word count using user and case fixed effects; raw semantic diversity is retained as a variant in this same outcome (pp. 11-12, Divergent Ideation; p. 9, Models 9-10). The paper reports raw semantic diversity correlated with word count at r = 0.943 (p. 12). Coding flexibility reflects the codebook's distinction between within-person ideational variety and across-person diversity; this is an embedding-based proxy, not a count of idea categories. Figure 1 also uses conversation-level Welch two-sample t-tests, without a reported participant-clustered correction for those figure tests (p. 8).

contrasts.reported: Word-count-adjusted semantic diversity, Model 10: coefficient 0.178***, clustered SE (0.032); *** p<0.001. Raw semantic diversity, Model 9: coefficient 1.4***, clustered SE (0.058); *** p<0.001. Figure 1 marks the adjusted measure *** (p<0.001). These are voice-minus-text associations, not randomized modality effects. The two illustrative transcripts have semantic diversity = 4.51 (text) and 5.82 (voice); these are individual examples, not arm means.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Table 1, Models 9-10 and notes; p. 8, Figure 1; p. 4, Findings; p. 5, representative-interaction discussion

contrasts.reported: For the randomized voice-gender comparison, the paper states: "we find no evidence that AI persona affects any outcome variable." No outcome-specific coefficient, standard error, test statistic, p value, arm mean, or analyzed participant count is given. Female and male are labels for the two compared configurations; the paper designates neither as treatment or default control. This is a nested comparison within the spoken conversations, not a second independent sample.

outcomes.name: Within-conversation lexical diversity (word-count adjusted; raw and control-variable variants retained)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: All text measures use concatenated user messages only, excluding AI messages (p. 11, Text Extraction). One analysis observation is one conversation, with repeated conversations per student; the analytic sample contains 957 conversations from 203 students (p. 10, Descriptive Statistics). Table 1 uses OLS with user and case fixed effects and standard errors clustered by user and case (pp. 9 and 12, Statistical Analyses). Shannon entropy of the word-frequency distribution measures lexical repetition within a user's conversation. The paper names word-count-residualized lexical diversity as its primary repetition outcome; residualization uses user and case fixed effects. Unadjusted entropy and the specification including word count as a covariate are variants of this same outcome. Raw lexical diversity correlates with word count at r = 0.801 (p. 11, Repetition). It is not similarity between different people's outputs, so it is coded other/with_ai. Direction below follows the primary adjusted specification; the raw specification has the opposite sign. Figure 1 uses conversation-level Welch tests (p. 8).

contrasts.reported: Word-count-adjusted lexical diversity, Model 8: coefficient -0.042*, clustered SE (0.018); * p<0.05. Raw lexical diversity, Model 7: coefficient 0.262***, clustered SE (0.023); *** p<0.001. The appendix reports a word-count-control specification as beta = -0.105, p < 0.001 and describes it as substantively identical/equivalent; it supplies no SE for that coefficient. Figure 1 marks the adjusted measure *** (p<0.001), based on Welch tests rather than Table 1's fixed-effects regressions. The appendix coefficient and Table 1 coefficient are preserved separately as printed.

sample_overlap.locator: pp. 2-3, Approach: this manuscript describes its CAiSEY course dataset without identifying an earlier paper whose participants it reanalyzes. The modality and nested voice-gender contrasts use the same dataset, not independent samples.

company_involvement.description: No company involvement is disclosed. CAiSEY was developed in-house; the named support is the AI in Business Initiative at Columbia Business School, and the authors declare no competing interest. The underlying model provider is not named.
company_involvement.locator: p. 2, Approach; p. 6, Acknowledgments; p. 7, Competing Interests

eligibility.reason: The fully reported modality comparison is observational: students selected voice or text, and the paper expressly disclaims randomized modality assignment (p. 3, Approach; p. 10, Modality Switching). The study analyzed 203 people after exclusions (p. 10), and originality and within-conversation ideational breadth were computed from their own output (pp. 9 and 11-12), meeting the sample and output criteria. However, perceived male/female AI voice was randomly assigned within the spoken condition (pp. 3 and 10), and the authors state that no outcome differed by persona (p. 5). That nested comparison could be an eligible randomized ai_design contrast; the PDF does not specify its assignment unit/repeated-user allocation sufficiently to verify individual or randomized within-person-order assignment, or give its distinct analyzed people and outcome-specific results. The 218 male-voice and 240 female-voice counts are conversations (p. 10), not people. The main sample is well above the threshold, and 186 of 203 users explicitly used both modalities (p. 3), but no exact participant count for the gender analysis should be invented. Core is held unclear for the nested comparison; none of the numerical voice-versus-text effects should enter a randomized core estimate.

one_line_finding: Among 203 analyzed students, self-selected voice rather than text debate with CAiSEY was associated with greater word-count-adjusted within-conversation semantic breadth (coefficient 0.178, clustered SE 0.032, p<0.001; p. 9, Table 1, Model 10; participant count p. 10).
open_questions: For the nested randomized voice-gender comparison, was assignment made per participant or per conversation, and what allocation/order procedure applied to repeated users? Outcome-specific results and distinct analyzed people are not supplied (randomization: pp. 3 and 10; qualitative null result: p. 5). This determines whether that comparison, separately from observational modality effects, qualifies for core ai_design evidence.

Table 1 Model 8 reports adjusted lexical diversity coefficient -0.042 (SE 0.018), p<0.05, while the appendix describes a word-count-control specification as equivalent/substantively identical but prints beta = -0.105, p < 0.001 (pp. 9 and 11). The discrepancy is preserved, not resolved by recomputation.

The PDF does not name the underlying generative model/version or supply a data/code repository URL, although it says anonymized data and code are available (pp. 2-3 and 6). The saved PDF also gives no explicit manuscript version/date (p. 1).
notes: Read all 16 PDF pages and all 44,000 characters of the markdown conversion, including Supporting Information and transcripts. Outcome inventory from Figure 1 and Table 1: lexical dissimilarity from the case, semantic dissimilarity from the case, user message count, total user word count, unique user word count, TTR, lexical diversity, and semantic diversity. The 10 regression columns become 8 outcomes because raw and word-count-adjusted lexical/semantic variants are grouped (form rule 7); no substantive output-measure family is omitted. The one dataset is kept as one study; the main observational modality analysis and nested randomized voice-gender comparison are explicitly distinguished, with gender contrasts retaining only the qualitative result printed on p. 5. The four named arm entries are nested labels, not four mutually exclusive person groups. Table 1 calls N = 458 and N = 499 users, but Figure 1 and p. 10 explicitly identify those Ns as conversations; participant-arm counts therefore remain null. No measure compares different people's outputs, so no across_people outcome is coded, and AI remains available during production of every scored output. Within-conversation semantic breadth is flexibility; within-conversation lexical repetition is other. No delayed/unassisted task is reported. Switching checks and confidence/persuasion prompts in example transcripts are not separately analyzed output outcomes. Figure 1's Welch tests treat conversations as observations; the table instead clusters SEs by user and case. Regression coefficients are recorded in their raw printed scales, without computed effects or CIs. Data/code availability is asserted on p. 6 without a repository link; the demo on p. 12 is not a data/code source. No other screening form was opened.
